title: Major Metals and Their Ores
description: The metals that built civilization — and the minerals they come from

concepts.title: Iron, Aluminium, Copper
concepts.contentHtml:
Three metals dominate global production by tonnage:

  • Iron — extracted overwhelmingly from hematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄). Annual world production ~2.5 billion tonnes of ore. Underpins the steel industry — without it, no skyscrapers, ships, railways, or cars.
  • Aluminium — extracted from bauxite, a residual rock formed by tropical weathering. Bauxite is a mixture of aluminium hydroxides (gibbsite, böhmite, diaspore). Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the crust but was effectively unobtainable until the Hall-Héroult electrolytic process (1886) made it cheap.
  • Copper — primary ore is chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂), with secondary minerals like bornite and chalcocite. Mined mainly from huge low-grade porphyry deposits — entire mountains where copper is locked up at concentrations of just 0.4–1 %.

concepts.title: Precious and Specialty Metals
concepts.contentHtml:
Gold typically occurs as native metal — pure flecks of Au — in hydrothermal quartz veins or as alluvial grains eroded from those veins into river gravels (placer deposits). Average crustal abundance is just 4 parts per billion.

Silver occurs as native silver, argentite (Ag₂S), and as a by-product of lead-zinc mining (galena often carries percent-level silver).

Platinum-group metals (PGMs — platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium, ruthenium) come almost entirely from a few layered intrusions, especially the Bushveld Complex in South Africa, which holds ~75 % of world platinum reserves.

Tin is mined from cassiterite (SnO₂); nickel from sulfides like pentlandite and from lateritic weathering deposits; zinc from sphalerite (ZnS); lead from galena (PbS).

concepts.title: Critical Metals of the Energy Transition
concepts.contentHtml:
Decarbonisation has elevated a new tier of metals:

  • Lithium — battery cathodes and electrolytes. From hard-rock spodumene (Australia) and lithium-rich brines (Chile, Argentina, Bolivia — the 'Lithium Triangle').
  • Cobalt — battery cathode stabiliser. ~70 % comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo as a copper by-product.
  • Nickel — high-energy-density cathodes (NMC, NCA). Indonesia and the Philippines dominate laterite production.
  • Rare-earth elements (REEs) — neodymium and dysprosium for permanent magnets in EVs and wind turbines. Mined chiefly from bastnäsite and monazite; China holds ~60 % of mining and ~90 % of refining.
  • Graphite, manganese, vanadium — battery anodes, alloys, grid-scale flow batteries.

Securing supply of these metals is now treated as a strategic priority by governments and major industrial firms.

title: How Ore Deposits Form
description: The geological processes that concentrate metals enough to be mined

concepts.title: Magmatic and Hydrothermal Deposits
concepts.contentHtml:
Most economic ore deposits owe their existence to fluids — either silicate magmas or hot watery solutions — that selectively transport and concentrate metals.

Magmatic deposits: as a magma cools, dense sulfide droplets can separate and settle, scavenging chalcophile metals (Cu, Ni, PGMs). The Bushveld Complex (South Africa) and Sudbury (Canada — partly impact-modified) are the world's prime examples.

Hydrothermal deposits: hot water — often heated by a buried intrusion or by deep circulation along a fault — leaches metals from large rock volumes and redeposits them when conditions change (cooling, boiling, pH shift, redox change). Most of the world's gold, silver, copper, lead, zinc, tin, and tungsten arrive this way.

The textbook hydrothermal style is the porphyry copper deposit: a stockwork of fine quartz-sulfide veins around the cooling top of a granitic pluton, mined as enormous open pits 1–4 km across. Chuquicamata (Chile) and Bingham Canyon (Utah) are classic examples.

concepts.title: Sedimentary and Surficial Deposits
concepts.contentHtml:
Some of the largest ore bodies form not from magma or hydrothermal fluids but at and near Earth's surface:

  • Banded iron formations (BIFs) — laid down between 3.0 and 1.8 billion years ago when rising oxygen in the early oceans caused dissolved iron to precipitate as alternating layers of hematite/magnetite and chert. The Pilbara (Australia), Carajás (Brazil), and the Lake Superior region (USA/Canada) supply most of the world's iron from BIFs.
  • Laterites and bauxites — formed by intense tropical chemical weathering. Soluble elements wash away, leaving residual aluminium oxides (bauxite) or nickel/cobalt oxides and silicates (Ni laterites).
  • Placer deposits — formed by physical sorting in rivers and beaches; dense, weathering-resistant minerals like gold, cassiterite, platinum, and zircon accumulate in gravel bars. The Witwatersrand basin (South Africa) is a fossil placer that produced ~40 % of all gold ever mined.
  • Evaporite deposits — salt, potash, and lithium brines crystallise as enclosed basins dry up (Atacama, Salar de Uyuni).

concepts.title: Concentration Factors
concepts.contentHtml:
To be economic, an ore must concentrate the target metal far above its average crustal abundance. The required concentration factor varies enormously:

  • Iron: average crust 5 %, ore grade ~30–60 % → factor ~6–12×.
  • Copper: average crust 60 ppm, modern porphyry ore 0.4 % → factor ~70×.
  • Gold: average crust 4 ppb, mineable grade ~1–5 g/t → factor ~250–1,250×.
  • Lithium: average crust 20 ppm, hard-rock ore 1–2 % Li → factor ~500–1,000×.

Geology only delivers ore where natural processes happen to concentrate metals far beyond these baselines — which is rare. Most of the planet has no ore at all. The economics of mining are therefore an exploration problem first, an engineering problem second.

title: Mining Methods
description: Open pit, underground, placer, in-situ — how ore is actually extracted

concepts.title: Surface (Open-Pit) Mining
concepts.contentHtml:
Open-pit mining is the dominant method for large, low-grade deposits near the surface. A widening series of stepped benches is excavated, with rock broken by blasting and hauled out by trucks the size of houses (240-tonne capacity is routine).

The world's largest open pits include:

  • Bingham Canyon, Utah — 4 km wide, 1.2 km deep — the largest human excavation by volume, producing copper, gold, silver, molybdenum.
  • Chuquicamata, Chile — copper, ~4.3 km long, ~3 km wide, 1 km deep.
  • Mir Mine, Russia — diamond pit so deep that helicopters were banned over it because the air column drew them in.

Strip mining is a variant for tabular near-surface deposits like coal and oil sands: long parallel cuts that progressively expose and remove the ore. Reclamation — restoring the surface afterwards — is a major regulatory and engineering issue.

concepts.title: Underground Mining
concepts.contentHtml:
When ore is too deep to strip economically, mining moves underground. The choice of method depends on ore body geometry, rock strength, and grade:

  • Room-and-pillar — leaves columns of ore standing to support the roof. Suited to flat, bedded deposits like potash and trona.
  • Cut-and-fill — excavate a horizontal slice, backfill with waste rock and cement, mine the next slice up. High recovery but slow.
  • Sublevel stoping — drill rings of long blast holes from sublevels, blast outward into a central void (the stope). Standard for steep, narrow vein deposits.
  • Block caving — undercut a column of ore so it collapses under its own weight; draw the broken rock from below. Cheap per tonne, only viable in massive low-grade ore bodies.

The deepest gold mines in South Africa (e.g. Mponeng) reach about 4 km below surface, where rock temperatures exceed 60 °C and seismic risk is constant.

concepts.title: Placer, In-Situ, and Frontier Methods
concepts.contentHtml:
Placer mining — exploits gravitational sorting in river gravels. Methods range from artisanal panning and sluicing to industrial dredges floating on ponds, scooping gravel and washing out gold, tin, or platinum on shaker tables.

In-situ recovery (ISR) — instead of extracting rock, you extract the metal in solution. Boreholes inject lixiviant (e.g. dilute sulfuric acid, sodium carbonate, or oxygenated water) into the deposit; the pregnant solution is pumped back up and the metal recovered. Standard for uranium in sandstone-hosted deposits and for some copper oxide ores. Lower surface footprint than open-pit mining, but only suitable in permeable, isolated rock.

Heap leaching — broken ore is piled on an impermeable pad and sprayed with leach solution that percolates through, dissolving the metal. Used for low-grade gold (cyanide leach), copper (acid), and uranium.

Deep-sea mining — collecting polymetallic nodules from the abyssal Clarion-Clipperton Zone (Pacific) is being trialled but remains controversial because of unknown ecological impact.

title: Extraction and Refining
description: Turning ore into metal — pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning

concepts.title: Beneficiation — Concentrating the Ore
concepts.contentHtml:
Crude ore is rarely fed straight into a smelter. First it is upgraded — beneficiation:

  • Crushing and grinding down to the grain size at which metal-bearing minerals are physically separated from gangue.
  • Gravity separation — using density (jigs, spirals, shaking tables) for heavy minerals like cassiterite, gold, magnetite.
  • Magnetic separation — for magnetite iron ore and to remove magnetic impurities.
  • Froth flotation — the workhorse of modern mineral processing. The ground ore is mixed with water, frothing agents, and chemical 'collectors' that selectively make sulfide minerals hydrophobic. Air bubbles carry the sulfides to a froth on top, while gangue sinks. Invented in the early 1900s, flotation is the reason it is economic to mine 0.4 %-Cu ore.

The output is a concentrate typically running 25–35 % copper, 60 %+ iron, or comparable upgrades for other metals.

concepts.title: Pyrometallurgy
concepts.contentHtml:
Pyrometallurgy uses heat to drive chemical reduction.

Iron: hematite or magnetite + coke + limestone in a blast furnace at ~1500 °C. Coke is the reducing agent (CO from C + O₂). The output is pig iron at ~95 % Fe with 4 % C, refined further in basic-oxygen or electric-arc furnaces into steel.

Copper: sulfide concentrate is roasted to drive off some sulfur, then smelted to matte (Cu₂S + FeS), then converted by blowing air through it to oxidise iron and burn off remaining sulfur, producing blister copper (~99 %). Electrolytic refining brings it to 99.99 %.

Smelting is enormously energy-intensive and historically a major source of SO₂ pollution; modern smelters capture it as sulfuric acid.

concepts.title: Hydrometallurgy and Electrowinning
concepts.contentHtml:
Hydrometallurgy dissolves the metal into aqueous solution, then recovers it.

  • Leaching — copper oxide ores: dilute sulfuric acid; gold: dilute cyanide; uranium: sulfuric acid or alkaline carbonate; bauxite: hot caustic soda (the Bayer process — 1888).
  • Solvent extraction (SX) — selectively transfers the metal ion from leach solution into an organic solvent, then back into a clean aqueous strip solution.
  • Electrowinning (EW) — passing current through the strip solution deposits pure metal on cathode plates. The standard for copper, zinc, nickel, cobalt; also the Hall-Héroult cell for aluminium (electrolysing alumina dissolved in molten cryolite at ~960 °C — by far the largest single use of electricity in metallurgy).

Final purity tricks: electrolytic refining (used for the vast majority of commercial copper), the Mond process (volatile Ni(CO)₄ for nickel), and zone refining for ultra-pure semiconductor silicon.

title: World Production and Geopolitics
description: Where the metals come from — and why supply is concentrated

concepts.title: Top Producers Today
concepts.contentHtml:
For most metals, two or three countries dominate primary production:

  • Iron ore — Australia (~37 %) and Brazil (~17 %). Both are mining ancient banded iron formations.
  • Copper — Chile (~24 %) and Peru (~10 %). Both sit on the Andean porphyry copper belt.
  • Aluminium (bauxite) — Australia, Guinea, China.
  • Nickel — Indonesia (>50 %), the Philippines, Russia.
  • Cobalt — DR Congo (~70 %).
  • Lithium (mined) — Australia (spodumene), Chile (brines), China.
  • Rare earths — China (~60 % of mining, ~90 % of separation/refining).
  • Gold — broadly distributed: China, Russia, Australia, Canada, USA, South Africa.
  • Platinum — South Africa (~70 %).

This concentration reflects geology, not policy: deposits form in specific tectonic settings, and you can only mine where Earth has placed ore.

concepts.title: Reserves, Resources, and Reserve Lifetimes
concepts.contentHtml:
It helps to keep three categories straight:

  • Resource — total amount of a metal that geological evidence suggests exists in the ground at any grade.
  • Reserve — the subset of resources that can be extracted economically with current technology and prices.
  • Production — what is actually mined per year.

Reserves and resources are not fixed numbers — they grow with new exploration and technology and with rising prices that turn previously sub-economic mineralisation into ore. Despite headlines about 'running out of copper', global copper reserves have increased for decades because exploration has consistently outpaced extraction.

However, flow constraints are real. Even if reserves are large, the time required to find, permit, build, and ramp up a new mine is typically 10–20 years. Demand spikes — from EVs, grid-scale storage, defence — can outrun the metal industry's ability to respond.

concepts.title: Recycling, Externalities, and the Future
concepts.contentHtml:
Recycling already supplies a major share of base metal demand:

  • Lead — over 60 % of consumption is recycled (mostly from car batteries).
  • Steel — ~30 % of new steel comes from scrap; electric-arc furnaces are growing.
  • Copper — ~30 % from scrap.
  • Aluminium — recycling uses about 5 % of the energy of primary smelting; well-collected streams are nearly fully recycled.

Recycling will not be enough alone — primary mining has to expand to feed the energy transition — but a circular economy reduces the new ore tonnage required.

Externalities are central to the modern picture: tailings dam failures (Brumadinho 2019, ~270 dead), acid mine drainage, water consumption in arid mining regions, biodiversity loss, indigenous land rights, artisanal cobalt mining and child labour in the DRC. The next century of mining will be judged less on tonnes produced and more on how those externalities are managed.
